# Point Estimation {.section-slide}

Guessing a parameter from a sample.

## Where do we need a guess?

::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.box}
**Polls.** What share of voters support a candidate?
:::
::: {.box}
**Finance.** What is the expected return of a stock?
:::
::: {.box}
**Demography.** How many children does a woman have on average?
:::
::: {.box}
**War.** How many weapons does the enemy produce?
:::
::: {.box}
**Ecology.** How many fish are there in a lake?
:::
::: {.box}
**Our class.** What share of students have ever cheated?
:::
:::

## Point estimator

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
Let $\theta$ be a population parameter. A statistic $\hat{\theta}$ used to guess or estimate $\theta$ is called an **estimator** of $\theta$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Note</span>
Estimator is not a particular numerical guess, but a rule or a procedure of arriving at a guess from the sample. A different sample gives a different guess.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
$\bar{X}$ is an estimator of $\mu$
:::
::: {.box .c}
$s^2$ is an estimator of $\sigma^2$
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
But you can come up with different guesses. What makes **a good guess**, and when one guess is **better** than another? We need some **criteria** to compare estimators.
:::

## Criteria 1: Unbiased estimator

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
If $E(\hat{\theta})=\theta$, then $\hat{\theta}$ is an **unbiased** estimator of $\theta$. That is your guess is unibiased, if it is right on average.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c .xp #xp1-card onclick="xpShow('xp1')"}
$\bar{X}$ is unbiased for $\mu$
:::
::: {.box .c .xp #xp2-card onclick="xpShow('xp2')"}
$s^2$ is unbiased for $\sigma^2$
:::
:::

::: {.cap}
Click an example.
:::

::: {.box .xpd #xp1}
$\bar{X}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ is a **random variable**: a different sample gives a different $\bar{X}$. Its expected value is
$$E(\bar{X})=E\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right]=\mu$$
:::

::: {.box .xpd #xp2}
$s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar{X})^2$ is a **random variable**: a different sample gives a different $s^2$. Its expected value is
$$E(s^2)=E\!\left[\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar{X})^2\right]=\sigma^2$$

If we divide by $n$ instead of $n-1$, the variance estimator becomes **biased**.
:::

<script>
function xpShow(id) {
  ['xp1', 'xp2'].forEach(function (k) {
    document.getElementById(k).classList.toggle('on', k === id && !document.getElementById(k).classList.contains('on'));
    document.getElementById(k + '-card').classList.toggle('sel', document.getElementById(k).classList.contains('on'));
  });
}
</script>


# Example: randomized response {.section-slide}

Asking a sensitive question

## A sensitive question

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Question</span>
Have you ever cheated during your studies at NU?
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
People may **refuse** to answer, or **lie**. We want **anonymity**, but we have **no technical way** to guarantee it.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Solution: **randomized response**. Add randomness, so that no single answer reveals the truth.
:::

## The idea

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">The rule</span>
If you were born in **January, February or March**, answer **"Yes"**, whatever the truth.<br>
Otherwise, answer **truthfully**. Asking respondents to **flip a coin** before answering is another way to randomize.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
The person who collects the answers **does not know your birth month**. So a "Yes" may be forced by the rule: it does **not** reveal that you cheated.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
Each respondent keeps **some anonymity**. But the answers are now a mix of forced and true ones.
:::

## How do we estimate the truth?

::: {.box}
We observe only the **share of "Yes" answers**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Parameter</span>
$p=$ the true share of students who **cheated**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
How do we recover $p$ from the data, when some of the "Yes" answers are not true?
:::

## Our class survey

::: {.box}
Question: **Have you ever cheated during your studies at NU?** Rule: born in January, February or March, answer "Yes"; otherwise truthfully.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c .warn}
<span class="tag">"No"</span>
60%
:::
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">"Yes"</span>
40%
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
What is your guess for $p$, the true share of students who cheated? Is it 40%, more, or less?
:::

## Working out the estimator

::: {.box}
About $\tfrac{3}{12}=\tfrac14$ of people are forced to say "Yes"; the other $\tfrac34$ answer truthfully:
$$P(\text{Yes})=\tfrac14\cdot 1+\tfrac34\cdot p$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
Solve for $p$ and replace $P(\text{Yes})$ by the observed share $\hat{y}$:
$$\hat{p}=\frac{\hat{y}-\frac14}{\frac34}$$
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">Unbiased</span>
$E(\hat{y})=P(\text{Yes})$, so $E(\hat{p})=p$
:::
::: {.box .key .c}
<span class="tag">Our data</span>
$\hat{p}=\dfrac{0.40-0.25}{0.75}=0.20$
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
About 20% cheated. The price of privacy: the standard error is $\approx7.4$ points, against $\approx4.5$ if we could ask directly.
:::

# Example: German tanks {.section-slide}

World War II

## Estimating tank production

::: {.box}
The Allies wanted to estimate German tank production $a$ from the **serial numbers** $X_i$ of captured tanks.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Allied intelligence used traditional methods (spies). Statisticians analyzed serial numbers.
:::

. . .

| Date | Intelligence | Statisticians | Actual |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| June 1941 | 1,550 | 244 | **271** |
| August 1942 | 1,550 | 327 | **342** |

## A simple model

::: {.box}
Serial numbers of captured tanks are uniform: $X_i\sim U[0,a]$. We want to estimate the maximum $a$, which is the total number of tanks.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">One tank, $n=1$</span>
Since $E[X_1]=\frac{a}{2}$, the guess $\hat{\theta}=X_1$ is **biased**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
Fix: $\hat{\theta}_{1}=2X_1$. Then $E[2X_1]=2\cdot\frac{a}{2}=a$: **unbiased**.
:::

## Many tanks

::: {.box}
With $n>1$ tanks we can use the sample mean: $\hat{\theta}_{\text{mean}}=2\bar{X}$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
$E[2\bar{X}]=2E[\bar{X}]=2\cdot\frac{a}{2}=a$: also **unbiased**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
Two unbiased estimators: $2X_1$ and $2\bar{X}$. **Which one is better?**
:::

## Which is better?

::: {.box}
We say "better" means smaller **variance**.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">One observation</span>
$$\operatorname{Var}(2X_1)=4\cdot\frac{a^2}{12}=\frac{a^2}{3}$$
:::
::: {.box .key .c}
<span class="tag">Sample mean</span>
$$\operatorname{Var}(2\bar{X})=4\cdot\frac{a^2/12}{n}=\frac{a^2}{3n}$$
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
$\operatorname{Var}(2\bar{X})=\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Var}(2X_1)$: using all the data is **$n$ times more efficient**.
:::

## Criteria 2: Efficiency

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
Among unbiased estimators, the one with the **smaller variance** is more **efficient**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .xp #int-card onclick="intToggle()"}
<span class="tag">Intuition (click)</span>
Variance is the expected **squared error** of a guess. Both estimators are right on average, but the one with lower variance is much more likely to be close to the truth in a single sample.
:::

::: {.box .good .xpd #int-detail}
For an unbiased estimator $E(\hat{\theta})=\theta$, so
$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta})=E\big[(\hat{\theta}-E(\hat{\theta}))^2\big]=E\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big]$$
This is the **expected squared mistake** of the guess. To make this mistake as small as possible, we want the **smallest variance**.
:::

<script>
function intToggle() {
  var d = document.getElementById('int-detail'), c = document.getElementById('int-card');
  d.classList.toggle('on'); c.classList.toggle('sel', d.classList.contains('on'));
}
</script>

## Simulating the tank problem

<svg id="tk-svg" viewBox="0 0 900 330" class="famplot"></svg>

<div class="readout" id="tk-out"></div>

<div class="ctl" style="justify-content:center">
  <button class="act ghost" id="tk-b1"></button>
  <button class="act ghost" id="tk-b2"></button>
  <button class="act ghost" id="tk-b3"></button>
  <button class="act ghost" id="tk-b4"></button>
  <button class="act" id="tk-run">Run again</button>
  <span>Sample size $n$: <span class="seg" id="tk-n"><button data-n="5">5</button><button data-n="10" class="on">10</button><button data-n="50">50</button><button data-n="100">100</button></span></span>
</div>

<div class="cap">Each histogram is scaled to its own peak: compare the widths.</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var N = 10, REPS = 1000, X0 = 0, X1 = 2, BW = 0.02, NB = Math.round((X1 - X0) / BW);
  var EST = {
    e1: { name: "2X₁", col: "#2b6cb0" },
    e2: { name: "2X̄", col: "#2f855a" },
    e3: { name: "(n+1)/n · max", col: "#dd6b20" },
    e4: { name: "max Xᵢ", col: "#805ad5" }
  };
  var KEYS = ["e1", "e2", "e3", "e4"], on = { e1: false, e2: false, e3: false, e4: false }, res = null;
  function sim() {
    var r = { e1: [], e2: [], e3: [], e4: [] };
    for (var k = 0; k < REPS; k++) {
      var s = 0, mx = 0, first = 0;
      for (var i = 0; i < N; i++) { var u = Math.random(); if (i === 0) first = u; s += u; if (u > mx) mx = u; }
      r.e1.push(2 * first); r.e2.push(2 * s / N); r.e3.push((N + 1) / N * mx); r.e4.push(mx);
    }
    return r;
  }
  function stats(a) {
    var m = a.reduce(function (s, x) { return s + x; }, 0) / a.length;
    var v = a.reduce(function (s, x) { return s + (x - m) * (x - m); }, 0) / (a.length - 1);
    return [m, Math.sqrt(v)];
  }
  var svg = document.getElementById("tk-svg"), out = document.getElementById("tk-out");
  var L = 60, R = 870, T = 40, B = 270;
  function hx(x) { return L + (x - X0) / (X1 - X0) * (R - L); }
  function draw() {
    var cnt = {}, mxk = {}, g = "";
    KEYS.forEach(function (k) {
      var c = []; for (var b = 0; b < NB; b++) c.push(0);
      res[k].forEach(function (x) { var b = Math.floor((x - X0) / BW); if (b >= 0 && b < NB) c[b]++; });
      cnt[k] = c; mxk[k] = Math.max.apply(null, c);
    });
    g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + B + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + B + '" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
    for (var x = 0; x <= 2; x += 0.5) g += '<text x="' + hx(x) + '" y="' + (B + 24) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" fill="#52606d">' + x.toFixed(1) + '</text>';
    g += '<text x="' + ((L + R) / 2) + '" y="' + (B + 52) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#1f2933">estimate of a (true a = 1, n = ' + N + ')</text>';
    var shown = KEYS.filter(function (k) { return on[k]; });
    shown.forEach(function (k) {
      cnt[k].forEach(function (n, b) {
        var h = n / mxk[k] * (B - T - 10);
        g += '<rect x="' + (hx(X0 + b * BW) + 0.5) + '" y="' + (B - h) + '" width="' + ((R - L) / NB - 1) + '" height="' + h + '" fill="' + EST[k].col + '" opacity="0.55"/>';
      });
    });
    g += '<line x1="' + hx(1) + '" y1="' + (T - 10) + '" x2="' + hx(1) + '" y2="' + B + '" stroke="#1b3a5c" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/>';
    shown.forEach(function (k, i) {
      g += '<rect x="' + (R - 190) + '" y="' + (T - 30 + i * 24) + '" width="16" height="16" fill="' + EST[k].col + '" opacity="0.6"/><text x="' + (R - 168) + '" y="' + (T - 17 + i * 24) + '" font-size="18" fill="#1f2933">' + EST[k].name + '</text>';
    });
    svg.innerHTML = g;
    out.innerHTML = shown.length ? shown.map(function (k) { var s = stats(res[k]); return EST[k].name + ": mean <b>" + s[0].toFixed(2) + "</b>, SD <b>" + s[1].toFixed(2) + "</b>"; }).join(" &nbsp;·&nbsp; ")
                                 : "Click an estimator to show the histogram of its guesses.";
  }
  function paint() {
    KEYS.forEach(function (k, i) {
      var b = document.getElementById("tk-b" + (i + 1));
      b.textContent = EST[k].name;
      b.style.background = on[k] ? EST[k].col : "#e4e7eb";
      b.style.color = on[k] ? "#fff" : "#323f4b";
    });
  }
  KEYS.forEach(function (k, i) {
    document.getElementById("tk-b" + (i + 1)).onclick = function () { on[k] = !on[k]; paint(); draw(); };
  });
  document.getElementById("tk-run").onclick = function () { res = sim(); draw(); };
  var nb = document.querySelectorAll("#tk-n button");
  nb.forEach(function (b) {
    b.onclick = function () {
      N = +b.getAttribute("data-n");
      nb.forEach(function (x) { x.classList.toggle("on", x === b); });
      res = sim(); draw();
    };
  });
  res = sim(); paint(); draw();
})();
</script>

## Better still

::: {.box .key}
$$\hat{\theta}_{\max}=\frac{n+1}{n}\cdot\max(X_i)$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
It is also **unbiased**, and its variance is much smaller: $\operatorname{Var}=\frac{a^2}{n(n+2)}$. In the simulation, it is the most efficient of the unbiased estimators.
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
Which estimator is best depends on the assumed population distribution.
:::

## Criteria 3: Consistency

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Definition</span>
An estimator is **consistent** if it converges to the true parameter as $n\to\infty$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
For this, both the **bias** and the **variance** must shrink to zero as $n\to\infty$.
:::

## Consistency: remarks

::: {.cards}
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Biased but consistent</span>
The error in small samples disappears with more data. Examples: the variance estimator that divides by $n$; $\max(X_i)$ for the upper bound $a$ of a Uniform, since $E[\max]=\frac{n}{n+1}a<a$, but the bias $-\frac{a}{n+1}$ and the variance both go to $0$.
:::
::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">Unbiased but inconsistent</span>
Centered on the truth, but the uncertainty never shrinks. Example: using only $X_1$ to estimate $a$.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
Consistency is the "large sample minimum": we often tolerate small-sample bias if we reach the truth with enough data.
:::

## Three properties

| Property | Focus | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Unbiasedness** | Accuracy | On target **on average** |
| **Consistency** | Reliability | Error disappears as $n\to\infty$ |
| **Efficiency** | Precision | **Smallest error** among competitors |

. . .

::: {.box .key}
An ideal estimator is **unbiased, consistent and efficient**. Among unbiased and consistent estimators we pick the most efficient: narrower confidence intervals, more powerful tests.
:::

## Properties depend on the population

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Remark</span>
To **establish** these properties we need **assumptions about the population distribution**. The same estimator may have a property under one model and lose it under another.
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">Needs a specific model</span>
$2X_1$ and $2\bar{X}$ are unbiased for $a$ **assuming** $X_i\sim U[0,a]$. If the population were Normal, $E[2\bar{X}]=2\mu\neq a$.<br><br>Efficiency: $2\bar{X}$ is beaten by $\frac{n+1}{n}\max(X_i)$ for Uniform, but $\bar{X}$ is the most efficient for Normal.
:::
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">Holds for (almost) any population</span>
$E[\bar{X}]=\mu$ and $E[s^2]=\sigma^2$: unbiased whenever the mean (variance) exists and the sample is i.i.d.<br><br>$\bar{X}\to\mu$ as $n\to\infty$: consistent for any population with a finite mean (Law of Large Numbers).
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
Always ask: **under what assumption** is this property true?
:::

## The sample mean for $\mu$

::: {.box .key}
In many problems the parameter we want is a mean $\mu$, so we use $\bar{X}$. How good is it?
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Bias</span>
$\bar{X}$ is **always unbiased** for $\mu$: Normal, Binomial, Poisson, anything.
:::
::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">Efficiency</span>
$\bar{X}$ is **not always the most efficient**. For a Uniform population, the maximum-based estimator beats it.
:::
:::

## Where we use $\bar{X}$

::: {.cards}
::: {.box}
**Polls.** The share of supporters is the mean of the 0/1 answers: $\hat{p}=\bar{X}$.
:::
::: {.box}
**Finance.** The expected return $\mu$ of a stock is estimated by the average of past returns.
:::
::: {.box}
**Medicine.** The mean drop in blood pressure is estimated by the average over the patients.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">Other estimators are needed</span>
**Ecology.** How many fish are there in a lake?<br>
**Demography.** How many children does a woman have on average?<br>
**War.** How many weapons does the enemy produce?<br>
**Our class.** What share of students have ever cheated?
:::

# Interval Estimation {.section-slide}

From a guess to a range of plausible values.

## From point to interval

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Main question</span>
What can we infer about $\mu$ from a simple random sample?
:::

. . .

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .good}
Our guess $\bar{X}$ is **unbiased**: on average it equals $\mu$.
:::
::: {.box .good}
It is **consistent**: it becomes more precise as $n$ grows.
:::
:::

## Consistency of the sample mean

::: {.figure-slide}
![](est_Code_Generated_Image%20(6).png){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.cap}
Fair die: the distribution of $\bar{X}$ narrows around $\mu=3.5$ as $n$ grows.
:::

## Same estimator, different precision

::: {.box}
For $n=10$, $20$ and $200$ we use the **same estimator** $\bar{X}$, and it is centred at $\mu$ every time.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
But with $n=200$ the guess is **much more precise**: its variance is lower, as we saw before.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
A single number does not tell us **how precise** the guess is. We need a way to **communicate the uncertainty** of our guess. 
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
One way is to report also a variance or standard error along with the estimator, but we can do even better with an **interval estimate**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
An **interval estimate** captures the uncertainty around our guess.
:::

## Confidence intervals in research

::: {.figure-slide}
![](est_Screenshot%202026-04-20%20at%2008.57.03.png){fig-align="center"}
:::

::: {.cap}
Allcott et al. (2020): effect of deactivating Facebook for one month on well-being.
:::

## How to read the figure

::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">The zero line</span>
The baseline: the **control group**, who kept using Facebook as usual.
:::
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">The dots: point estimates</span>
The average change for the **treatment group** (those who quit). To the right of zero: they felt better.
:::
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">The bars: confidence intervals</span>
Our uncertainty. If the bar does not cross zero, the effect is "statistically significant" at the 95% level. If it crosses zero, we cannot tell a real change from noise.
:::
:::

## Interval estimate

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Idea</span>
An **interval estimate** (confidence interval) is a range of values, computed from the sample, that are **reasonable guesses** for an unknown parameter.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Here we consider interval estimates of the **population mean $\mu$** only.
:::

## Our assumption

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Assumption</span>
The population standard deviation $\sigma$ is **known**: the only uncertainty is about $\bar{X}$. Later we drop this.
:::

## Example: Which values of $\mu$ are plausible?

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Example: a die</span>
Observed $\bar{X}=3$. Population variance $\sigma^2=2.92$, sample size $n=20$. Standard error: $SE=\sqrt{2.92/20}\approx 0.382$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">Question</span>
If the true mean were $\mu$, how likely is it to observe $\bar{X}=3$ **or something more extreme**?
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
"More extreme" = in the tails, at least as far from $\mu$ as $\bar{X}$ is.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">CLT</span>
To answer, we use the distribution of $\bar{X}$ **given $\mu$**. By the CLT it is approximately normal:
$$\bar{X}\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$$
:::

## How surprising is $\bar{X}=3$ given a specific $\mu$?

<svg id="pv-svg" viewBox="0 0 900 283" class="famplot"></svg>

<div class="readout" style="color:#c53030;font-weight:700;font-size:0.95em">Probability of $\bar{X}$ at least this far from $\mu$ (red area): <span id="pv-p"></span></div>

<div class="readout" id="pv-st" style="min-height:2.6em"></div>

<div class="ctl" style="justify-content:center">
  <label>Hypothesized $\mu$: <input type="range" id="pv-mu" min="1" max="5" step="0.01" value="2.2" style="width:340px"> <b id="pv-mu-val">2.20</b></label>
  <span>Significance level $\alpha$: <span class="seg" id="pv-a"><button data-a="0" class="on">none</button><button data-a="0.10">10%</button><button data-a="0.05">5%</button><button data-a="0.01">1%</button></span></span>
</div>

<div class="ctl" id="pv-jump" style="justify-content:center;visibility:hidden">
  <button class="act ghost" id="pv-jl">$\mu$ → lower end of CI</button>
  <button class="act ghost" id="pv-ju">$\mu$ → upper end of CI</button>
</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var SE = Math.sqrt(2.92 / 20), XO = 3, L = 50, R = 880, XA = 0, XB = 6;
  var TOP = 10, SC = 270 / 1.4;                                     // y from 1.25 (top) to -0.15
  var Z = { "0.1": [1.645, "#440154", "90%"], "0.05": [1.96, "#21918c", "95%"], "0.01": [2.576, "#fde725", "99%"] };
  var mu = 2.2, alpha = 0;
  function px(x) { return L + (x - XA) / (XB - XA) * (R - L); }
  function py(y) { return TOP + (1.1 - y) * SC; }
  function pdf(x, m) { return Math.exp(-0.5 * Math.pow((x - m) / SE, 2)) / (SE * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)); }
  function erf(x) { var s = x < 0 ? -1 : 1; x = Math.abs(x); var t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * x);
    return s * (1 - (((((1.061405429 * t - 1.453152027) * t) + 1.421413741) * t - 0.284496736) * t + 0.254829592) * t * Math.exp(-x * x)); }
  function Phi(z) { return 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / Math.SQRT2)); }
  var svg = document.getElementById("pv-svg"), sl = document.getElementById("pv-mu"), lab = document.getElementById("pv-mu-val"),
      st = document.getElementById("pv-st"), jump = document.getElementById("pv-jump");
  function path(m, lo, hi) {
    var d = "M" + px(lo).toFixed(1) + "," + py(0).toFixed(1);
    for (var x = lo; x <= hi + 1e-9; x += 0.01) d += " L" + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(pdf(x, m)).toFixed(1);
    return d + " L" + px(hi).toFixed(1) + "," + py(0).toFixed(1) + " Z";
  }
  function draw() {
    var m = mu, dist = Math.abs(XO - m), p = 2 * (1 - Phi(dist / SE)), g = "";
    lab.textContent = m.toFixed(2);
    var lo = Math.max(XA, m - 4 * SE), hi = Math.min(XB, m + 4 * SE);
    g += '<defs><clipPath id="pv-clip"><rect x="' + L + '" y="0" width="' + (R - L) + '" height="232"/></clipPath>' +
         '<pattern id="pv-hatch" width="8" height="8" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse" patternTransform="rotate(45)"><rect width="8" height="8" fill="#fff4e5"/><line x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="8" stroke="#dd6b20" stroke-width="3.5"/></pattern></defs><g clip-path="url(#pv-clip)">';
    var zc = alpha ? Z[String(alpha)][0] : 0, cut = zc * SE;
    if (alpha) {                                                    // fixed-area rejection tails (alpha/2 each)
      g += '<path d="' + path(m, lo, Math.min(m - cut, hi)) + '" fill="url(#pv-hatch)"/>';
      g += '<path d="' + path(m, Math.max(m + cut, lo), hi) + '" fill="url(#pv-hatch)"/>';
    }
    if (m - dist > lo) g += '<path d="' + path(m, lo, Math.min(m - dist, hi)) + '" fill="#c53030" fill-opacity="0.45"/>';
    if (m + dist < hi) g += '<path d="' + path(m, Math.max(m + dist, lo), hi) + '" fill="#c53030" fill-opacity="0.45"/>';
    var d = "";
    for (var x = lo; x <= hi + 1e-9; x += 0.01) d += (d ? " L" : "M") + px(x).toFixed(1) + "," + py(pdf(x, m)).toFixed(1);
    g += '<path d="' + d + '" fill="none" stroke="#444" stroke-width="2.5"/>';
    if (alpha) [m - cut, m + cut].forEach(function (c) {
      g += '<line x1="' + px(c) + '" y1="' + py(pdf(c, m)) + '" x2="' + px(c) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#dd6b20" stroke-width="2.5"/>';
    });
    g += '</g>';
    g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + py(0) + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
    for (var t = 0; t <= 6; t++) g += '<text x="' + px(t) + '" y="' + (py(0) + 20) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#52606d">' + t + '</text>';
    g += '<line x1="' + px(XO) + '" y1="' + TOP + '" x2="' + px(XO) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="3"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (px(XO) + (m < XO ? 8 : -8)) + '" y="' + (TOP + 14) + '" text-anchor="' + (m < XO ? "start" : "end") + '" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">X̄ = 3</text>';
    g += '<line x1="' + px(m) + '" y1="' + TOP + '" x2="' + px(m) + '" y2="' + py(0) + '" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (px(m) + (m < XO ? -8 : 8)) + '" y="' + (TOP + 14) + '" text-anchor="' + (m < XO ? "end" : "start") + '" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">μ = ' + m.toFixed(2) + '</text>';
    document.getElementById("pv-p").textContent = p.toFixed(4);
    if (!alpha) {
      st.innerHTML = 'Choose a significance level α to see which values of μ are plausible.';
    } else {
      var c = Z[String(alpha)], a = alpha, lowE = XO - cut, upE = XO + cut, edge = Math.abs(dist - cut) < 1e-4, inside = dist < cut && !edge;
      var y = 267;
      g += '<line x1="' + px(lowE) + '" y1="' + y + '" x2="' + px(upE) + '" y2="' + y + '" stroke="' + c[1] + '" stroke-width="8"/>';
      g += '<text x="' + (px(lowE) - 10) + '" y="' + (y + 5) + '" text-anchor="end" font-size="15" fill="#52606d">' + lowE.toFixed(2) + '</text>' +
           '<text x="' + (px(upE) + 10) + '" y="' + (y + 5) + '" text-anchor="start" font-size="15" fill="#52606d">' + upE.toFixed(2) + '</text>';
      g += '<circle cx="' + px(Math.min(XB, Math.max(XA, m))) + '" cy="' + y + '" r="9" fill="' + (edge ? "#dd6b20" : (inside ? "#2f855a" : "#c53030")) + '" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="2.5"/>';
      var verdict = edge ? '<b>on the boundary</b>' :
        (inside ? '<b style="color:#2f855a">plausible</b>' : '<b style="color:#c53030">not plausible</b>');
      st.innerHTML = 'α = ' + (a * 100).toFixed(0) + '%: each tail has area ' + (a / 2) + '; cutoffs at μ ± ' + cut.toFixed(2) + '. ' +
        'X̄ = 3 is ' + (edge ? 'exactly at the cutoff, so p = α' : (inside ? 'inside, so p ≥ α' : 'in the tail, so p &lt; α')) + '.<br>' +
        'μ = ' + m.toFixed(2) + ' is ' + verdict + ': ' + (edge ? 'at the end of' : (inside ? 'inside' : 'outside')) + ' the ' + c[2] + ' CI [' + lowE.toFixed(2) + ', ' + upE.toFixed(2) + '].';
    }
    svg.innerHTML = g;
    jump.style.visibility = alpha ? "visible" : "hidden";
  }
  function setMu(v) { mu = v; sl.value = v; draw(); }
  sl.addEventListener("input", function () { mu = +sl.value; draw(); });
  var ab = document.querySelectorAll("#pv-a button");
  ab.forEach(function (b) { b.onclick = function () {
    alpha = +b.getAttribute("data-a");
    ab.forEach(function (x) { x.classList.toggle("on", x === b); });
    draw();
  }; });
  document.getElementById("pv-jl").onclick = function () { if (alpha) setMu(XO - Z[String(alpha)][0] * SE); };
  document.getElementById("pv-ju").onclick = function () { if (alpha) setMu(XO + Z[String(alpha)][0] * SE); };
  draw();
})();
</script>

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
If you understand this figure, then you understand the primary logic of statistical inference.
:::

## Key result

::: {.box}
The shaded area is the probability of a sample mean **at least as extreme** as $\bar{X}=3$, if the slider value were the true $\mu$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
As $\mu$ moves away from $\bar{X}$, this probability shrinks: such an $\bar{X}$ becomes unlikely, so far-away values of $\mu$ are **less plausible**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
Confidence interval = the values of $\mu$ for which this probability is **larger than $\alpha$**: the plausible values given our data.
:::

## An interval around $\mu$

::: {.box}
Find an interval around $\mu$ that contains $\bar{X}$ with probability $1-\alpha$:
$$P(\mu-\text{margin}\le\bar{X}\le\mu+\text{margin})=1-\alpha$$
$\alpha$ is the **significance level**: the probability of falling outside.
:::

. . .

::: {.figure-slide}
![](est_Code_Generated_Image%20(6)%20copy.png){fig-align="center" height=330}
:::

## Finding the margin

::: {.box}
Standardize $\bar{X}$, dividing by the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$:
$$P\!\left(-\tfrac{\text{margin}}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\le Z\le\tfrac{\text{margin}}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\right)=1-\alpha$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Define $z_{\alpha/2}$ by $P(-z_{\alpha/2}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$. Then
$$\text{margin}=z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$$
:::

## Flipping the inequality

::: {.box}
$$P\!\left(\mu-z_{\alpha/2}\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\le\bar{X}\le\mu+z_{\alpha/2}\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right)=1-\alpha$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
The same event, written for $\mu$:
$$P\!\left(\bar{X}-z_{\alpha/2}\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\le\mu\le\bar{X}+z_{\alpha/2}\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right)=1-\alpha$$
:::

## Confidence interval for $\mu$

::: {.box .key}
<span class="tag">$\sigma$ known</span>
$$CI_{1-\alpha}=\left[\bar{X}-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\ \bar{X}+z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right]$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
The random interval $\bar{X}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$ contains $\mu$ with probability $1-\alpha$. If we repeat the sampling many times, about a fraction $1-\alpha$ of the intervals contain $\mu$.
:::

## The parts of the interval

::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Critical value $z_{\alpha/2}$</span>
The point of the standard normal $N(0,1)$ with area $\alpha/2$ in each tail.
:::
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$</span>
The standard deviation of $\bar{X}$.
:::
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Margin of error $z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$</span>
Half the width of the interval: how many standard errors we go out from $\bar{X}$.
:::
:::

## Example: girls' heights

::: {.box}
Heights of girls in our class:
$n=185$, $\bar{X}=165.9$ cm, and $\sigma=8.7$ cm is assumed **known**.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
Estimate a **90% confidence interval** for the true mean height.
:::

## Computing the 90% interval

::: {.cards}
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Critical value</span>
$\alpha=0.10$, so $z_{0.05}\approx1.645$
:::
::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Standard error</span>
$SE=\frac{8.7}{\sqrt{185}}\approx0.640$
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Margin of error</span>
$ME=1.645\times0.640\approx1.053$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
$$CI_{0.90}=165.9\pm1.053=[164.85,\ 166.95]$$
:::

## Interpreting the interval

::: {.box}
If we took many samples of 185 girls and built an interval from each, about **90%** of them would contain the true mean height $\mu$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
<span class="tag">Plausibility</span>
$164$ cm is outside the interval. If the true mean were $164$, a sample mean as high as $165.9$ would be very unlikely, so we exclude it from the plausible values.
:::

## Common critical values

| Confidence level | $\alpha$ | Tail area $\alpha/2$ | Critical value $z_{\alpha/2}$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| 90% | 0.10 | 0.05 | **1.645** |
| 95% | 0.05 | 0.025 | **1.960** |
| 99% | 0.01 | 0.005 | **2.576** |

. . .

::: {.box}
The critical value $z_{\alpha/2}$ bounds the upper $\alpha/2$ proportion of the standard normal.
:::

## Precision vs. confidence

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">95% interval</span>
$165.9\pm1.96\cdot0.640$<br>$=[164.65,\ 167.15]$
:::
::: {.box .c}
<span class="tag">99% interval</span>
$165.9\pm2.576\cdot0.640$<br>$=[164.25,\ 167.55]$
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.figure-slide}
![](est_Code_Generated_Image%20(6)%20copy%203.png){fig-align="center" height=220}
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
More confidence needs a larger critical value, so the interval gets **wider**.
:::

## What drives the width?

::: {.box}
The width is set by the margin of error $ME=z_{\alpha/2}\,\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$.
:::

| Factor | Change | Width | Precision |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Sample size $n$ | $\uparrow$ | **narrows** | **increases** |
| Confidence level | $\uparrow$ | **widens** | **decreases** |
| Population SD $\sigma$ | $\uparrow$ | **widens** | **decreases** |

## The power of $n$

::: {.box .key}
$n$ is the only lever that raises **both** precision and confidence.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Since $n$ sits under a square root in the standard error, you must **quadruple $n$** to cut the interval width in half.
:::

## Choose your interval

<svg id="cg-svg" viewBox="0 0 900 250" class="famplot"></svg>

<div class="cg-stats">
  <div class="cg-big"><b id="cg-pct">–</b><span id="cg-pct-l">of the intervals contain μ</span></div>
  <div class="cg-w"><i class="dot blue"></i><span>Your width</span><b id="cg-wy"></b></div>
  <div class="cg-w"><i class="dot orange"></i><span>Exact CI width</span><b id="cg-wc"></b></div>
</div>

<div class="cg-ctl">

  <button class="act ghost" id="cg-match">Match the CI</button>

</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var N = 240, PL = 215, PR = 850, CX = 105, YC = 125, YT = 12, YB = 238, HALF = 4.5;   // half-range of the axis, in standard errors
  var Z = { "0.1": 1.645, "0.05": 1.96, "0.01": 2.576 };
  var EX = [
    { what: "hours of sleep per night", who: "students", unit: "hour", sd: 1, yl: "hours", n: 25, a: 0.10, mu: [6.5, 7.5] },
    { what: "weekly study time", who: "students", unit: "hours", sd: 4, yl: "hours", n: 16, a: 0.05, mu: [8, 14] },
    { what: "daily commute to campus", who: "students", unit: "minutes", sd: 10, yl: "minutes", n: 25, a: 0.01, mu: [25, 45] },
    { what: "score on the final exam", who: "students", unit: "points", sd: 10, yl: "points", n: 100, a: 0.05, mu: [60, 75] },
    { what: "height", who: "women", unit: "cm", sd: 8, yl: "cm", n: 64, a: 0.10, mu: [160, 170] },
    { what: "daily screen time", who: "students", unit: "hours", sd: 2, yl: "hours", n: 16, a: 0.01, mu: [4, 6] }
  ];
  var S = { k: -1 }, drag = false, raf = null;
  var svg = document.getElementById("cg-svg"), sl = {}, runB = document.getElementById("cg-run");
  function gauss() { var u = 1 - Math.random(), v = Math.random(); return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * v); }
  function ypu() { return (YC - YT - 6) / (HALF * S.se); }                       // pixels per data unit
  function yv(v) { return YC - (v - S.mu) * ypu(); }
  function sample() { S.xs = []; for (var i = 0; i < N; i++) S.xs.push(S.mu + S.se * gauss()); }
  function hits() { var c = 0; for (var i = 0; i < N; i++) if (Math.abs(S.xs[i] - S.mu) <= S.w) c++; return c; }
  function nice(raw) { var mag = Math.pow(10, Math.floor(Math.log(raw) / Math.LN10)), c = [1, 2, 5, 10]; for (var i = 0; i < 4; i++) if (c[i] * mag >= raw) return c[i] * mag; return 10 * mag; }
  function nextEx() {
    S.k = (S.k + 1) % EX.length; var e = EX[S.k]; S.e = e;
    S.mu = Math.round((e.mu[0] + Math.random() * (e.mu[1] - e.mu[0])) * 10) / 10;
    S.se = e.sd / Math.sqrt(e.n); S.mci = Z[String(e.a)] * S.se;
    var f = Math.min([0.5, 0.65, 1.4, 1.6][Math.floor(Math.random() * 4)], 3.4 * S.se / S.mci); S.w = Math.round(f * S.mci / (S.se / 50)) * (S.se / 50); S.stage = 0;
    S.phase = 0; S.done = false; S.busy = false; S.shown = 0; S.g = 0; S.muFrac = 0; S.col = false;
    if (raf) cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
    var pct = Math.round((1 - e.a) * 100);
    document.getElementById("cg-story").innerHTML = 'You want to estimate the average <b>' + e.what + '</b> of ' + e.who + '. The population standard deviation is <b>σ = ' + e.sd + ' ' + e.unit + 
      '</b> (known). You will observe a random sample of <b>n = ' + e.n + '</b>. Choose an interval <b>X̄ ± m</b> that you expect to contain the true mean μ in <b>' + pct + '%</b> of samples.';
    render();
  }
  function picker() {
    var u = ypu(), m = S.w * u, c = S.mci * u, g = "";
    g += '<line x1="' + CX + '" y1="' + (YC - m) + '" x2="' + CX + '" y2="' + (YC + m) + '" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="3"/>';
    [-1, 1].forEach(function (s) {
      g += '<line x1="' + (CX - 11) + '" y1="' + (YC + s * m) + '" x2="' + (CX + 11) + '" y2="' + (YC + s * m) + '" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="4" stroke-linecap="round"/>';
      g += '<line x1="' + (CX - 36) + '" y1="' + (YC + s * c) + '" x2="' + (CX + 36) + '" y2="' + (YC + s * c) + '" stroke="#dd6b20" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>';
    });
    g += '<text x="' + (CX - 42) + '" y="' + (YC - c - 3) + '" text-anchor="end" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#dd6b20">exact CI</text>' +
         '<text x="' + (CX - 42) + '" y="' + (YC - c + 14) + '" text-anchor="end" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#dd6b20">±' + S.mci.toFixed(2) + '</text>';
    g += '<text x="' + (CX + 18) + '" y="' + (YC - m + 5) + '" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">m = ' + S.w.toFixed(2) + '</text>';
    g += '<circle cx="' + CX + '" cy="' + YC + '" r="6" fill="#1f2933"/>';
    g += '<text x="' + (CX + 12) + '" y="' + (YC + 5) + '" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">X̄</text>';
    return g;
  }
  function plot() {
    var g = '<rect x="' + (PL - 8) + '" y="4" width="' + (PR - PL + 16) + '" height="' + (YB - 0) + '" rx="12" fill="#f5f7fa"/>';
    g += '<text x="' + (PL + 4) + '" y="22" font-size="14" fill="#7b8794">' + S.e.yl + '</text>';
    if (!S.phase) {
      g += '<text x="' + ((PL + PR) / 2) + '" y="' + (YC + 6) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#7b8794">Press Run to draw ' + N + ' random samples</text>';
      return g;
    }
    var lo = S.mu - HALF * S.se, hi = S.mu + HALF * S.se, step = nice((hi - lo) / 6);
    for (var t = Math.ceil(lo / step) * step; t <= hi + 1e-9; t += step) {
      var y = yv(t); if (y < YT + 4 || y > YB - 2) continue;
      g += '<line x1="' + PL + '" y1="' + y + '" x2="' + PR + '" y2="' + y + '" stroke="#e4e7eb"/>' +
           '<text x="' + (PL - 14) + '" y="' + (y + 5) + '" text-anchor="end" font-size="14" fill="#7b8794">' + (Math.round(t * 100) / 100) + '</text>';
    }
    var pitch = (PR - PL) / N, m = S.w * ypu() * S.g;
    g += '<defs><clipPath id="cg-clip"><rect x="' + (PL - 8) + '" y="4" width="' + (PR - PL + 16) + '" height="' + YB + '" rx="12"/></clipPath></defs><g clip-path="url(#cg-clip)">';
    for (var i = 0; i < S.shown; i++) {
      var x = PL + (i + 0.5) * pitch, yy = yv(S.xs[i]), ok = Math.abs(S.xs[i] - S.mu) <= S.w;
      var col = S.col ? (ok ? "#5b8fd0" : "#c53030") : "#a9b8cb";
      if (m > 0.3) g += '<line x1="' + x.toFixed(1) + '" y1="' + (yy - m).toFixed(1) + '" x2="' + x.toFixed(1) + '" y2="' + (yy + m).toFixed(1) + '" stroke="' + col + '" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round"/>';
      g += '<circle cx="' + x.toFixed(1) + '" cy="' + yy.toFixed(1) + '" r="1.6" fill="#1f2933"/>';
    }
    g += '</g>';
    if (S.muFrac > 0) {
      var ym = yv(S.mu), xe = PL + (PR - PL) * S.muFrac;
      g += '<line x1="' + PL + '" y1="' + ym + '" x2="' + xe + '" y2="' + ym + '" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2.2"/>';
      if (S.muFrac >= 1) g += '<text x="' + (PR + 14) + '" y="' + (ym + 6) + '" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">μ</text>';
    }
    g += '<rect x="' + (PL + 2) + '" y="' + (YB - 30) + '" width="' + (S.col ? 372 : 124) + '" height="26" rx="8" fill="#f5f7fa" fill-opacity="0.94"/>';
    g += '<circle cx="' + (PL + 12) + '" cy="' + (YB - 14) + '" r="3" fill="#1f2933"/><text x="' + (PL + 22) + '" y="' + (YB - 9) + '" font-size="14" fill="#52606d">sample mean</text>';
    if (S.col) {
      g += '<circle cx="' + (PL + 132) + '" cy="' + (YB - 14) + '" r="5" fill="#5b8fd0"/><text x="' + (PL + 142) + '" y="' + (YB - 9) + '" font-size="14" fill="#52606d">interval contains μ</text>' +
           '<circle cx="' + (PL + 282) + '" cy="' + (YB - 14) + '" r="5" fill="#c53030"/><text x="' + (PL + 292) + '" y="' + (YB - 9) + '" font-size="14" fill="#52606d">misses μ</text>';
    }
    return g;
  }
  function render() {
    svg.innerHTML = plot() + picker();
    var w2 = function (x) { return (2 * x).toFixed(2); };
    document.getElementById("cg-wy").textContent = w2(S.w);
    document.getElementById("cg-wc").textContent = w2(S.mci);
    var p = document.getElementById("cg-pct"), l = document.getElementById("cg-pct-l");
    var tg = Math.round((1 - S.e.a) * 100);
    if (S.done) { var h = hits(); p.textContent = Math.round(100 * h / N) + "%"; l.textContent = "of " + N + " intervals contain μ · target " + tg + "%"; }
    else { p.textContent = "?%"; l.textContent = "of " + N + " intervals contain μ · target " + tg + "%"; }
    var CAP = ["Drag an end of the blue bar to set your margin m, then press Run.",
               "Each dot is the mean X̄ of one random sample.",
               "Your interval X̄ ± m is built around every sample mean.",
               "The true mean μ. Which intervals caught it?",
               "Each interval either catches μ or not. The percentage describes the method over many samples."];
    document.getElementById("cg-cap").textContent = CAP[S.stage || 0];
    runB.disabled = S.busy; runB.style.opacity = S.busy ? 0.5 : 1;
  }
  function setW(w) { if (S.busy) return; S.w = Math.max(0, Math.min(4 * S.se, Math.round(w / (S.se / 50)) * (S.se / 50))); render(); }
  function run() {
    if (S.busy) return;
    sample(); S.phase = 1; S.stage = 1; S.done = false; S.busy = true; S.shown = 0; S.g = 0; S.muFrac = 0; S.col = false;
    var D1 = 1500, D2 = 650, D3 = 600, D4 = 900, t0 = null;
    function ease(x) { return 1 - Math.pow(1 - x, 2); }
    function step(ts) {
      if (t0 === null) t0 = ts; var t = ts - t0;
      if (t < D1) { S.shown = Math.floor(N * ease(t / D1)); S.stage = 1; }
      else { S.shown = N;
        if (t < D1 + D2) { S.g = ease((t - D1) / D2); S.stage = 2; }
        else { S.g = 1;
          if (t < D1 + D2 + D3) { S.muFrac = (t - D1 - D2) / D3; S.stage = 3; }
          else { S.muFrac = 1; S.stage = 3;
            if (t >= D1 + D2 + D3 + D4) { S.col = true; S.done = true; S.busy = false; S.stage = 4; render(); return; } } } }
      render(); raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  }
  function pointerY(e) { var pt = svg.createSVGPoint(); pt.x = e.clientX; pt.y = e.clientY; return pt.matrixTransform(svg.getScreenCTM().inverse()); }
  svg.style.touchAction = "none";
  svg.addEventListener("pointerdown", function (e) { var p = pointerY(e); if (p.x < PL - 40 && !S.busy) { drag = true; svg.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); setW(Math.abs(p.y - YC) / ypu()); e.preventDefault(); } });
  svg.addEventListener("pointermove", function (e) { var p = pointerY(e); if (drag) setW(Math.abs(p.y - YC) / ypu()); svg.style.cursor = (drag || p.x < PL - 40) ? "ns-resize" : "default"; });
  svg.addEventListener("pointerup", function () { drag = false; });
  svg.addEventListener("pointercancel", function () { drag = false; });
  runB.onclick = run;
  document.getElementById("cg-match").onclick = function () { setW(S.mci); };
  document.getElementById("cg-new").onclick = nextEx;
  nextEx();
})();
</script>

## What the game shows

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">Wider</span>
Covers $\mu$ **more often** than needed, but the interval is less precise.
:::
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">Narrower</span>
Falls **below the target**: too many intervals miss $\mu$.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
The confidence interval $\bar{X}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ is the **narrowest** symmetric interval that still reaches coverage $1-\alpha$ in the long run.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Luck</span>
A single run of 240 samples is noisy. A slightly narrower interval can look fine once, and even the exact CI can land a little below target. Run again to see the coverage move around.
:::

# Example: student weight {.section-slide}

Two confidence intervals, and what their overlap means.

## Look at the data first

<svg id="wh-svg" viewBox="0 0 900 340" class="famplot"></svg>

<script>
(function () {
  var svg = document.getElementById("wh-svg"), L = 60, R = 860, T = 30, B = 270, X0 = 35, X1 = 125, BW = 5;
  var men = [0,0,2,2,8,28,30,21,18,15,8,7,2,2,2,0,0,1], nm = 146;
  var wom = [1,11,37,68,46,39,11,6,2,2,0,0,0,1,0,0,0,0], nw = 224;
  var YM = 32;
  function px(x) { return L + (x - X0) / (X1 - X0) * (R - L); }
  function py(y) { return B - y / YM * (B - T); }
  var g = '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + B + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + B + '" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
  for (var y = 0; y <= 30; y += 10) g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="' + py(y) + '" x2="' + R + '" y2="' + py(y) + '" stroke="#e4e7eb"/>' +
    '<text x="' + (L - 8) + '" y="' + (py(y) + 5) + '" text-anchor="end" font-size="15" fill="#52606d">' + y + '%</text>';
  for (var x = 40; x <= 120; x += 10) g += '<text x="' + px(x) + '" y="' + (B + 24) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#52606d">' + x + '</text>';
  g += '<text x="' + ((L + R) / 2) + '" y="' + (B + 54) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18" fill="#1f2933">weight (kg)</text>';
  [[wom, nw, "#dd6b20"], [men, nm, "#2b6cb0"]].forEach(function (s) {
    s[0].forEach(function (c, i) {
      if (!c) return;
      var h = c / s[1] * 100, x = X0 + i * BW;
      g += '<rect x="' + (px(x) + 1) + '" y="' + py(h) + '" width="' + (px(x + BW) - px(x) - 2) + '" height="' + (B - py(h)) + '" fill="' + s[2] + '" opacity="0.55"/>';
    });
  });
  [["#2b6cb0", "Men (n = 146)", 0], ["#dd6b20", "Women (n = 224)", 1]].forEach(function (c) {
    g += '<rect x="660" y="' + (T + c[2] * 26) + '" width="16" height="16" fill="' + c[0] + '" opacity="0.6"/><text x="684" y="' + (T + 13 + c[2] * 26) + '" font-size="18" fill="#1f2933">' + c[1] + '</text>';
  });
  svg.innerHTML = g;
})();
</script>

. . .

::: {.cap}
Share of each group in 5 kg bins. Women's weights are centred lower and are less spread out; men's are centred higher with a longer right tail.
:::

## The data

::: {.box}
Self-reported weights (kg) of ECON211 students over several semesters. As before, we **assume $\sigma$ is known** and take it equal to the sample SD of each group.
:::

| Group | $n$ | $\bar{X}$ | $\sigma$ | $SE=\sigma/\sqrt n$ |
|:--|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Men | 146 | 72.29 | 12.13 | 1.004 |
| Women | 224 | 55.16 | 7.93 | 0.530 |

. . .

::: {.box .key}
Estimate a **95% confidence interval** for the mean weight of men, and one for women.
:::

## 95% CI for men

::: {.box}
$z_{0.025}=1.96$, $\ SE=\dfrac{12.13}{\sqrt{146}}\approx1.004$, $\ ME=1.96\times1.004\approx1.97$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
$$CI_{0.95}^{\text{men}}=72.29\pm1.97=[70.32,\ 74.26]$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">Same data, but only $n=15$</span>
$SE=\dfrac{12.13}{\sqrt{15}}\approx3.132$, $\ ME=1.96\times3.132\approx6.14$
$$CI_{0.95}^{\text{men}}=72.29\pm6.14=[66.15,\ 78.43]$$
:::

## 95% CI for women

::: {.box}
$z_{0.025}=1.96$, $\ SE=\dfrac{7.93}{\sqrt{224}}\approx0.530$, $\ ME=1.96\times0.530\approx1.04$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
$$CI_{0.95}^{\text{women}}=55.16\pm1.04=[54.12,\ 56.20]$$
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">Same data, but only $n=15$</span>
$SE=\dfrac{7.93}{\sqrt{15}}\approx2.048$, $\ ME=1.96\times2.048\approx4.01$
$$CI_{0.95}^{\text{women}}=55.16\pm4.01=[51.15,\ 59.17]$$
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
The women's interval is narrower: smaller $\sigma$ and a larger $n$ give a smaller standard error.
:::

## Comparing the two intervals

<svg id="ci2-svg" viewBox="0 0 900 290" class="famplot"></svg>

<script>
(function () {
  var svg = document.getElementById("ci2-svg"), L = 60, R = 860, A = 45, B = 85;
  function px(x) { return L + (x - A) / (B - A) * (R - L); }
  var g = '';
  for (var t = 45; t <= 85; t += 5) g += '<line x1="' + px(t) + '" y1="20" x2="' + px(t) + '" y2="245" stroke="#e4e7eb"/>';
  g += '<line x1="' + L + '" y1="245" x2="' + R + '" y2="245" stroke="#52606d" stroke-width="2"/>';
  for (var t2 = 45; t2 <= 85; t2 += 5) g += '<text x="' + px(t2) + '" y="270" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#52606d">' + t2 + '</text>';
  [[72.29, 1.97, 55, "#2b6cb0", "Men, n = 146", 1],
   [72.29, 6.14, 110, "#2b6cb0", "Men, n = 15", 0.6],
   [55.16, 1.04, 165, "#dd6b20", "Women, n = 224", 1],
   [55.16, 4.01, 220, "#dd6b20", "Women, n = 15", 0.6]].forEach(function (c) {
    var y = c[2], x1 = px(c[0] - c[1]), x2 = px(c[0] + c[1]), col = c[3], o = c[5];
    g += '<g stroke="' + col + '" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round" opacity="' + o + '">' +
         '<line x1="' + x1 + '" y1="' + y + '" x2="' + x2 + '" y2="' + y + '"/>' +
         '<line x1="' + x1 + '" y1="' + (y - 9) + '" x2="' + x1 + '" y2="' + (y + 9) + '"/>' +
         '<line x1="' + x2 + '" y1="' + (y - 9) + '" x2="' + x2 + '" y2="' + (y + 9) + '"/></g>' +
         '<circle cx="' + px(c[0]) + '" cy="' + y + '" r="5" fill="' + col + '" opacity="' + o + '"/>' +
         '<text x="' + (x1 - 12) + '" y="' + (y + 5) + '" text-anchor="end" font-size="14" fill="#52606d">' + (c[0] - c[1]).toFixed(2) + '</text>' +
         '<text x="' + (x2 + 12) + '" y="' + (y + 5) + '" text-anchor="start" font-size="14" fill="#52606d">' + (c[0] + c[1]).toFixed(2) + '</text>' +
         '<text x="' + px(c[0]) + '" y="' + (y - 17) + '" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="' + col + '">' + c[4] + '</text>';
  });
  svg.innerHTML = g;
})();
</script>

. . .

::: {.box .key}
With the full samples the two intervals **do not overlap**: no value of $\mu$ is plausible for both groups at the same time.
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
With $n=15$ the intervals are **much wider** ($\pm6.14$ and $\pm4.01$): less data, less precision. They still do not overlap here, because the two means are about 17 kg apart.
:::

## What does overlap mean?

::: {.cards}
::: {.box .good .c}
<span class="tag">No overlap</span>
Every plausible mean for men is larger than every plausible mean for women. The means are very likely **different**: a test of equal means at this confidence level would find a **significant difference**.
:::
::: {.box .warn .c}
<span class="tag">Overlap</span>
Some values are plausible for **both** groups. The data **cannot rule out** equal means: the difference could be just noise.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.box}
Overlap means "**inconclusive**", not "the means are equal". With more data the intervals shrink and may separate. (Even slightly overlapping intervals can hide a significant difference: non-overlap is a sufficient, not a necessary, sign.)
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
A formal answer ("is the difference real?") comes with hypothesis testing. Intervals give the intuition.
:::

## Assumptions

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">What the intervals rely on</span>
Independent draws, and an approximately normal $\bar{X}$. By the CLT this is fine here ($n=146$ and $224$), even though weights are skewed.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .warn}
<span class="tag">What they do not capture</span>
Weights are **self-reported**, and the sample is **not random** (only ECON211 students). A large $n$ shrinks sampling error but does **not** remove selection or reporting bias.
:::

# Beyond the mean {.section-slide}

The same logic works for other estimators.

## Intervals for other estimators

::: {.box}
For the mean we used the distribution of $\bar{X}$ to build $\bar{X}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma/\sqrt n$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
The same idea works for **any estimator**: use its sampling distribution to say how far from the truth it is likely to be. The interval communicates the **uncertainty** of the guess.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .good}
How to derive such intervals is **outside the scope of this course**. Let us just look at two of our examples, with **95%** intervals.
:::

## Cheating: 95% interval

::: {.box}
Randomized response: $n=78$, observed share of "Yes" $\hat{y}=0.40$, so $\hat{p}=\dfrac{0.40-0.25}{0.75}=0.20$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
$$CI_{0.95}=[\,5.5\%,\ 34.5\%\,]$$
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
Wide: the forced "Yes" answers add noise. This is the price of privacy.
:::

## German tanks: 95% interval

::: {.box}
<span class="tag">Illustrative sample</span>
$n=10$ captured tanks, largest serial number $240$. Point estimate: $\dfrac{n+1}{n}\cdot240=264$.
:::

. . .

::: {.box .key}
$$CI_{0.95}=[\,241,\ 347\,]$$
:::

. . .

::: {.cap}
Not symmetric around the estimate: the largest tank can be at most $a$, so the data say more about the lower side than the upper side.
:::
